title: Turn on NCCL's own logging first
text: When a collective hangs or fails, rerun with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO, and add NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS (for example INIT,NET) to narrow it. The log shows which network transport and interfaces NCCL picked, which usually explains the failure.

title: Pin the bootstrap interface when a node has several
text: If NCCL picks the wrong network interface for its socket bootstrap, set NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME to the interface (or prefix) that the ranks can reach each other on, and confirm the choice in the NCCL_DEBUG=INFO output.

title: Give NCCL enough shared memory in containers
text: NCCL uses shared memory between processes on one node. A container's small default /dev/shm can make it fail; run with a larger shared memory size (or the host IPC namespace) as the troubleshooting guide describes.

title: Separate a topology problem from a network problem
text: Run the same job on a single node first. If it passes there and fails across nodes, look at the network path (interfaces, firewall rules, the network plugin); if it fails on one node too, look at the GPUs and their links.

title: Do not disable transports to make an error go away
text: Never leave NCCL_IB_DISABLE or NCCL_P2P_DISABLE set as a fix: they hide the fault and fall back to slower paths. Use them only to bisect which transport is failing, then fix that transport.

title: EFA needs a security group that allows itself
text: For EFA traffic between instances, the security group must allow all inbound and all outbound traffic to and from the security group itself.

title: Confirm the EFA device is visible before running a job
text: After installing the EFA software, check that the libfabric EFA provider sees the device with fi_info -p efa. If it lists nothing, fix the installation or the instance's network interface before debugging the application.

title: Count the EFA interfaces an instance actually has
text: Instance types support different numbers of network cards and EFA interfaces, and each EFA interface is attached at launch or while the instance is stopped. Check how many EFA interfaces were attached to an instance before expecting traffic on all of them.

title: Start a pod investigation with describe and events
text: For a pod that is Pending, CrashLoopBackOff or not Ready, run kubectl describe pod first: the Events section usually names the reason (scheduling, image pull, probe failure) before you read any application log.

title: Read the previous container's logs after a crash
text: When a container restarts, kubectl logs shows the new instance. Use kubectl logs --previous to see the output of the run that crashed.

title: CrashLoopBackOff is a symptom, not a cause
text: CrashLoopBackOff means the container keeps exiting and the kubelet is backing off between restarts. Find the exit code and the last log lines; the restart delay itself is not the problem.

title: Request GPUs as a limit on the extended resource
text: GPUs are requested through the device plugin's extended resource (for example nvidia.com/gpu) under limits; the cluster needs the vendor's device plugin for that resource to exist.

title: OOMKilled means the memory limit was reached
text: A container terminated with reason OOMKilled used more memory than its limit. Raise the limit or reduce the workload's memory; restarting it unchanged repeats the kill.

title: ImagePullBackOff: check the name, tag and pull secret
text: For ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull, check that the image name and tag exist, that the node can reach the registry, and that a private registry has an imagePullSecret the pod can use.

title: Look up Xid errors in the kernel log
text: NVIDIA driver errors appear in the kernel log as Xid messages with a number. Look the number up in NVIDIA's Xid catalogue to see whether it points at the application, the driver or the hardware.

title: Use nvidia-smi to see what each GPU is doing
text: nvidia-smi shows every GPU's utilisation, memory use, temperature and the processes holding it; nvidia-smi -q gives the full detail, including ECC error counts.

title: Run DCGM diagnostics on a suspect node
text: NVIDIA DCGM can run health checks and diagnostics on a node's GPUs; run them before putting a node back into service after unexplained GPU errors.

title: Containers need the NVIDIA Container Toolkit to see GPUs
text: A container sees no GPU unless the runtime is configured with the NVIDIA Container Toolkit. If nvidia-smi fails inside the container but works on the host, check the toolkit and runtime configuration.

title: CUDA out of memory: check caching before buying memory
text: PyTorch keeps freed GPU memory in a caching allocator. Use the memory statistics it exposes to see what is allocated versus reserved, and the PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF settings to reduce fragmentation.

title: CUDA calls are asynchronous
text: CUDA kernels run asynchronously, so an error can surface at a later, unrelated line. Set CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 while debugging to get the error at the call that caused it.

title: Every rank must join every collective
text: In torch.distributed, collectives must be called by all ranks of the process group in the same order; one rank skipping a call makes the others hang until the timeout.
